78fe7822dce4.before:
Title: Brewline Duo
Description: Brewline Duo

The Brewline Duo is our dual boiler espresso machine for home baristas who want to pull a shot and steam milk at the same time.

Most home machines use one boiler for both brewing and steaming, which means waiting for the temperature to swing up before you can froth milk. The Duo separates the two jobs. A small brew boiler feeds the group head, and a larger steam boiler runs the wand, so a flat white is one continuous motion instead of two.

Each boiler has its own PID controller. You set the brew temperature in half-degree steps from the front panel, and the steam boiler holds its own pressure independently. The group is a saturated 58 mm design, so it accepts standard baskets, tampers and distribution tools.

The rotary pump is quieter than a vibration pump and gives the same pressure from the first shot to the tenth. A needle valve on the side lets you ramp pressure for a gentle pre-infusion, or leave it fully open for a classic nine bar profile. The shot timer starts automatically when you lift the lever.

If you are new to espresso, start with 18 grams in and about 36 grams out, then adjust the grind until the shot takes between 25 and 32 seconds. The Duo is forgiving here because the temperature does not drift while you experiment.

The four-hole steam tip produces dry steam within seconds of opening the valve. Texturing 200 ml of milk for a latte takes roughly 25 seconds. The wand is insulated, so you can wipe it with a cloth right after use without burning your fingers.

The water tank holds 2.5 litres and slides out from the front. Descale the brew boiler every few months depending on your water, and backflush the group weekly with a blind basket. Both boilers can be drained through a service port on the underside.

In our internal tests the brew boiler stayed within 0.4 °C of the set point across a 20-shot session. The machine reaches brewing temperature in 11 minutes from cold, and the steam boiler holds 1.2 bar. Peak power draw is 1,650 W. The brew boiler holds 0.8 litres and the steam boiler holds 1.5 litres.

“We designed the Duo for people who make two milk drinks every morning and don't want to wait between them,” said Brewline product lead Maya Ortiz.

The Brewline Duo costs $1,199 and comes with a three-year warranty on the boilers, pump and electronics.

Title: Solo
Description: The Solo from Brewline.

The Brewline Solo is a compact single boiler espresso machine with a PID controller, made for people starting out with espresso at home.

The Solo uses one 350 ml stainless boiler for both brewing and steaming. A PID controller keeps the brew temperature steady, which is the single biggest upgrade over the thermostat machines most people start with. It uses the same 58 mm portafilter as our larger machines, so accessories carry over when you upgrade.

The vibration pump is fitted with an over-pressure valve set to nine bar at the factory. That keeps shots from being pushed too hard, which is a common cause of harsh, bitter espresso on budget machines.

Because there is one boiler, you brew first and then flip the steam switch. The boiler takes about 45 seconds to climb to steam temperature. For one or two cappuccinos a day this is a small wait. If you make several milk drinks back to back, a dual boiler machine like the Duo is the better fit.

The drip tray is deep enough for a full morning of shots, and the 1.8 litre tank fills from the top. The Solo fits under most kitchen cabinets at 33 cm tall.

It is ready to brew about four minutes after you switch it on. The Solo costs $449 and carries a two-year warranty.

1fa865d2cca6.before:
Title: Dialing in espresso
Description: 

Dialing in means adjusting your recipe until a coffee tastes the way it should. This is the process we use in the Brewline test kitchen.

Pick a dose and a ratio and keep them fixed while you change the grind. A good starting point for a double basket is 18 grams of coffee in and 36 grams of liquid espresso out, a 1:2 ratio. Weigh both. Guessing by volume hides what is actually happening.

Pull a shot and time it from when the pump starts. If it runs faster than 25 seconds, grind finer. If it takes longer than 32 seconds, grind coarser. Taste each shot. Sour, thin espresso usually means under-extraction, so grind finer or raise the temperature a degree. Bitter, dry espresso usually means over-extraction, so grind coarser or shorten the ratio.

Only change one variable per shot. If you change the grind and the dose together, you cannot tell which one fixed the problem.

Distribute the grounds evenly before tamping. A few passes with a needle tool breaks up clumps and helps prevent channeling, where water finds a fast path through the puck and leaves the rest under-extracted. Tamp level. Tamping harder does not help once the bed is compressed.

Light roasts often taste best between 93 and 95 °C. Dark roasts can taste harsh at those temperatures and often do better between 88 and 91 °C. A machine with a PID lets you hold these settings reliably.

Title: Mill 64
Description: 

The Brewline Mill 64 is a single-dose flat burr grinder built for espresso and pour-over.

It uses 64 mm stainless flat burrs turning at a low speed, which keeps heat down and produces an even particle size. Adjustment is stepless, so you can make the very small changes espresso needs. The dial is marked so you can return to a pour-over setting and back without guessing.

You weigh your beans, pour them in, and grind the whole dose. A bellows on top pushes out the last grounds. We measured average retention below 0.2 grams, which means the coffee in your basket is the coffee you just weighed. Low retention matters most when you switch beans often or dial in a new bag.

An anti-static plate at the chute reduces clumping and mess, so the grounds fall straight into the dosing cup instead of sticking to the walls.

The Mill 64 grinds about 1.8 grams per second at espresso settings. It costs $329 and comes with a two-year warranty. The burrs are rated for roughly 500 kg of coffee before replacement.

22cef5b34a1f.before:
Title: Descaling
Description: Descaling.

Scale builds up inside boilers and pipes when hard water is heated. Descaling removes it before it blocks valves or damages heating elements.

It depends on your water. Test the hardness with a strip. Above 120 ppm, descale every two months. Between 60 and 120 ppm, every three to four months. Below 60 ppm, every four to six months is enough. Using filtered or blended water reduces how often you need to do it.

Use a citric acid descaler at about a 3 percent solution. Do not use vinegar. Vinegar is slow, leaves a smell, and the acetic acid is hard on brass fittings and gaskets. Never use a descaler in the steam boiler of a dual boiler machine unless the manual for your model says it is safe.

Empty the tank and fill it with the descaling solution. Run half of it through the group head and the hot water tap. Switch the machine off and let it sit for 20 minutes. Run the rest through, then rinse with two full tanks of fresh water. On the Duo, descale the brew boiler this way and leave the steam boiler to a service visit every two years.

If the machine is slow to heat up or the pump sounds strained, scale may already be restricting flow. Descale first, and contact support if the problem continues.

22cef5b34a1f.before:
Title: Descaling
Description: Descaling.

Scale builds up inside boilers and pipes when hard water is heated. Descaling removes it before it blocks valves or damages heating elements.

It depends on your water. Test the hardness with a strip. Above 120 ppm, descale every two months. Between 60 and 120 ppm, every three to four months. Below 60 ppm, every four to six months is enough. Using filtered or blended water reduces how often you need to do it.

Use a citric acid descaler at about a 3 percent solution. Do not use vinegar. Vinegar is slow, leaves a smell, and the acetic acid is hard on brass fittings and gaskets. Never use a descaler in the steam boiler of a dual boiler machine unless the manual for your model says it is safe.

Empty the tank and fill it with the descaling solution. Run half of it through the group head and the hot water tap. Switch the machine off and let it sit for 20 minutes. Run the rest through, then rinse with two full tanks of fresh water. On the Duo, descale the brew boiler this way and leave the steam boiler to a service visit every two years.

If the machine is slow to heat up or the pump sounds strained, scale may already be restricting flow. Descale first, and contact support if the problem continues.

1fa865d2cca6.before:
Title: Dialing in espresso
Description: 

Dialing in means adjusting your recipe until a coffee tastes the way it should. This is the process we use in the Brewline test kitchen.

Pick a dose and a ratio and keep them fixed while you change the grind. A good starting point for a double basket is 18 grams of coffee in and 36 grams of liquid espresso out, a 1:2 ratio. Weigh both. Guessing by volume hides what is actually happening.

Pull a shot and time it from when the pump starts. If it runs faster than 25 seconds, grind finer. If it takes longer than 32 seconds, grind coarser. Taste each shot. Sour, thin espresso usually means under-extraction, so grind finer or raise the temperature a degree. Bitter, dry espresso usually means over-extraction, so grind coarser or shorten the ratio.

Only change one variable per shot. If you change the grind and the dose together, you cannot tell which one fixed the problem.

Distribute the grounds evenly before tamping. A few passes with a needle tool breaks up clumps and helps prevent channeling, where water finds a fast path through the puck and leaves the rest under-extracted. Tamp level. Tamping harder does not help once the bed is compressed.

Light roasts often taste best between 93 and 95 °C. Dark roasts can taste harsh at those temperatures and often do better between 88 and 91 °C. A machine with a PID lets you hold these settings reliably.

Title: Brewline Duo
Description: Brewline Duo

The Brewline Duo is our dual boiler espresso machine for home baristas who want to pull a shot and steam milk at the same time.

Most home machines use one boiler for both brewing and steaming, which means waiting for the temperature to swing up before you can froth milk. The Duo separates the two jobs. A small brew boiler feeds the group head, and a larger steam boiler runs the wand, so a flat white is one continuous motion instead of two.

Each boiler has its own PID controller. You set the brew temperature in half-degree steps from the front panel, and the steam boiler holds its own pressure independently. The group is a saturated 58 mm design, so it accepts standard baskets, tampers and distribution tools.

The rotary pump is quieter than a vibration pump and gives the same pressure from the first shot to the tenth. A needle valve on the side lets you ramp pressure for a gentle pre-infusion, or leave it fully open for a classic nine bar profile. The shot timer starts automatically when you lift the lever.

If you are new to espresso, start with 18 grams in and about 36 grams out, then adjust the grind until the shot takes between 25 and 32 seconds. The Duo is forgiving here because the temperature does not drift while you experiment.

The four-hole steam tip produces dry steam within seconds of opening the valve. Texturing 200 ml of milk for a latte takes roughly 25 seconds. The wand is insulated, so you can wipe it with a cloth right after use without burning your fingers.

The water tank holds 2.5 litres and slides out from the front. Descale the brew boiler every few months depending on your water, and backflush the group weekly with a blind basket. Both boilers can be drained through a service port on the underside.

In our internal tests the brew boiler stayed within 0.4 °C of the set point across a 20-shot session. The machine reaches brewing temperature in 11 minutes from cold, and the steam boiler holds 1.2 bar. Peak power draw is 1,650 W. The brew boiler holds 0.8 litres and the steam boiler holds 1.5 litres.

“We designed the Duo for people who make two milk drinks every morning and don't want to wait between them,” said Brewline product lead Maya Ortiz.

The Brewline Duo costs $1,199 and comes with a three-year warranty on the boilers, pump and electronics.

Title: Descaling
Description: Descaling.

Scale builds up inside boilers and pipes when hard water is heated. Descaling removes it before it blocks valves or damages heating elements.

It depends on your water. Test the hardness with a strip. Above 120 ppm, descale every two months. Between 60 and 120 ppm, every three to four months. Below 60 ppm, every four to six months is enough. Using filtered or blended water reduces how often you need to do it.

Use a citric acid descaler at about a 3 percent solution. Do not use vinegar. Vinegar is slow, leaves a smell, and the acetic acid is hard on brass fittings and gaskets. Never use a descaler in the steam boiler of a dual boiler machine unless the manual for your model says it is safe.

Empty the tank and fill it with the descaling solution. Run half of it through the group head and the hot water tap. Switch the machine off and let it sit for 20 minutes. Run the rest through, then rinse with two full tanks of fresh water. On the Duo, descale the brew boiler this way and leave the steam boiler to a service visit every two years.

If the machine is slow to heat up or the pump sounds strained, scale may already be restricting flow. Descale first, and contact support if the problem continues.

Title: Descaling
Description: Descaling.

Scale builds up inside boilers and pipes when hard water is heated. Descaling removes it before it blocks valves or damages heating elements.

It depends on your water. Test the hardness with a strip. Above 120 ppm, descale every two months. Between 60 and 120 ppm, every three to four months. Below 60 ppm, every four to six months is enough. Using filtered or blended water reduces how often you need to do it.

Use a citric acid descaler at about a 3 percent solution. Do not use vinegar. Vinegar is slow, leaves a smell, and the acetic acid is hard on brass fittings and gaskets. Never use a descaler in the steam boiler of a dual boiler machine unless the manual for your model says it is safe.

Empty the tank and fill it with the descaling solution. Run half of it through the group head and the hot water tap. Switch the machine off and let it sit for 20 minutes. Run the rest through, then rinse with two full tanks of fresh water. On the Duo, descale the brew boiler this way and leave the steam boiler to a service visit every two years.

If the machine is slow to heat up or the pump sounds strained, scale may already be restricting flow. Descale first, and contact support if the problem continues.

Title: Dialing in espresso
Description: 

Dialing in means adjusting your recipe until a coffee tastes the way it should. This is the process we use in the Brewline test kitchen.

Pick a dose and a ratio and keep them fixed while you change the grind. A good starting point for a double basket is 18 grams of coffee in and 36 grams of liquid espresso out, a 1:2 ratio. Weigh both. Guessing by volume hides what is actually happening.

Pull a shot and time it from when the pump starts. If it runs faster than 25 seconds, grind finer. If it takes longer than 32 seconds, grind coarser. Taste each shot. Sour, thin espresso usually means under-extraction, so grind finer or raise the temperature a degree. Bitter, dry espresso usually means over-extraction, so grind coarser or shorten the ratio.

Only change one variable per shot. If you change the grind and the dose together, you cannot tell which one fixed the problem.

Distribute the grounds evenly before tamping. A few passes with a needle tool breaks up clumps and helps prevent channeling, where water finds a fast path through the puck and leaves the rest under-extracted. Tamp level. Tamping harder does not help once the bed is compressed.

Light roasts often taste best between 93 and 95 °C. Dark roasts can taste harsh at those temperatures and often do better between 88 and 91 °C. A machine with a PID lets you hold these settings reliably.

Title: Descaling
Description: Descaling.

Scale builds up inside boilers and pipes when hard water is heated. Descaling removes it before it blocks valves or damages heating elements.

It depends on your water. Test the hardness with a strip. Above 120 ppm, descale every two months. Between 60 and 120 ppm, every three to four months. Below 60 ppm, every four to six months is enough. Using filtered or blended water reduces how often you need to do it.

Use a citric acid descaler at about a 3 percent solution. Do not use vinegar. Vinegar is slow, leaves a smell, and the acetic acid is hard on brass fittings and gaskets. Never use a descaler in the steam boiler of a dual boiler machine unless the manual for your model says it is safe.

Empty the tank and fill it with the descaling solution. Run half of it through the group head and the hot water tap. Switch the machine off and let it sit for 20 minutes. Run the rest through, then rinse with two full tanks of fresh water. On the Duo, descale the brew boiler this way and leave the steam boiler to a service visit every two years.

If the machine is slow to heat up or the pump sounds strained, scale may already be restricting flow. Descale first, and contact support if the problem continues.
